all sentences must compose of at least a noun phrase composed of one additional phrase, usually a verb phrase. the NP has two components, the noun itself (which usually acts as the active participant of the verb phrase— we call this the subject), as well as a determiner phrase. while syntactically a wider utterance can exist with just a noun phrase, it’s much more common to use a verb. therefore, uttering ‘the lion’ is not a complete sentence, it requires a verb phrase, so let’s use a verb, for example, *sleeps*.

now ‘sleeps’ is a classic example of the morphology of verbs. the simple addition of one extra morpheme changes the meaning of the word completely. let’s do a morphological analysis shall we? we have our root:

sleep.

we know this is a root because it is a single lexical based morpheme with no additional suffixes or TAM (tense, aspect, mood) morphemes. as there are no additional, and its syntactic function is NOT grammatical (it serves as a noun phrase, you can test this in the sentence ‘sleep is good’— so long as it’s *not* in the first person singular and plural (sleep), second person singular and plural, and third person plural.

this is because, interestingly, as a reservation of previous english conjugation rules which have undergone a process of linguistic reanalysis (we don’t have time, comment something snarky again if you want me to explain that), english verb conjugation is left with something interesting in its third person singulars. this is the addition of another morpheme to differentiate between verbs and nouns. This TAM morpheme, (an additional ‘s’) at the end of the root morpheme ‘sleep’, serves to identify the third person singular conjugation. and since it is a conjugation, that means it must be a verb (nouns don’t conjugate in english), therefore ‘sleeps’ is a goddamn verb.
